activities.caption: call the compliance rate with no police force
activities.name: ilComplyEstimate

config.prompt: No world police — yet what share of state conduct that international law addresses is compliant?
config.why: About 90 per cent: aircraft land on schedule under its rules, ambassadors are protected by them, most wars end within them — reciprocity, reputation, domestic institutions and the mutual interest of 195 states do the work a sovereign would.
config.context: The discipline's real subject is a mechanism, not a rule list — successes and celebrated failures are the same design at different stakes.

activities.anchor: Article 38 of the ICJ Statute is the field's constitution
activities.caption: pair each source with what makes it bind
activities.name: ilSourcesMatch

config.prompt: The rulebook's shelves — pair each source with what makes it bind:

pairs.right: consent: signature and ratification under pacta sunt servanda (Vienna Convention, 1969)
consistent state practice plus opinio juris — binding without signature
peremptory norms above everything: genocide, slavery, torture, aggression
good faith, estoppel, res judicata — borrowed from domestic systems to fill gaps
declarations and guidelines — the weather from which future custom precipitates

config.why: Treaty interpretation is a codified craft — VCLT Articles 31–32: ordinary meaning in context, in light of object and purpose; text plus telos, not will-hunting.

activities.anchor: The persistent objector rule makes this sound plausible
activities.caption: run the objection before the norm crystallises
activities.name: ilObjectorBranch

config.root: A new customary norm on maritime zones is crystallising, and your state dislikes it. Your legal team weighs its options.

start.text: When can dissent keep a state outside a customary norm?

choices.label: Consistently, from the first stirrings through the entire formation
choices.feedback: The narrow door: the objection must run through the custom's entire formation.

choices.label: Any time — announce disagreement whenever convenient
choices.feedback: Too late: announcing after the norm has crystallised changes nothing.

choices.label: Never needed — norms bind everyone equally without exception
choices.feedback: Not quite: an escape hatch exists — but narrow, and only during formation.

out.text: Your state may stay outside the new maritime-zone norm. One caveat remains:

choices.label: Does the same work against the genocide prohibition?
choices.feedback: No — and the boundary is the one that matters.

late.text: The objection fails: formation has ended, the norm binds.

choices.label: What should the team have done?
choices.feedback: Object consistently during formation — and know the jus cogens limit.

cogens.text: Against jus cogens — genocide, slavery, torture, aggression — nothing works: non-derogable and binding all states, signatory or not.

config.why: Contrast the two fates: a state may stay outside a new maritime-zone norm by objecting during formation, yet is bound by the genocide prohibition without ever signing anything.

activities.anchor: The puzzle first: why obey at all?
activities.caption: file each observation under its mechanism
activities.name: ilMechanismBuckets

config.prompt: Obedience without a sovereign — file each observation under the mechanism it illustrates:

items.label: one violation licenses another — tit-for-tat in consular access and fishing zones
a violator pays in credibility before markets, allies, creditors and courts (Guzman)
courts and legislatures implement what was signed — compliance as a by-product of governance
constituencies who sue their own governments (the European human-rights engine)
treaty performance as an exchange relationship
repeat players investing in future dealings

config.why: Where stakes turn existential — great-power security, territory, regime survival — the stack's grip fails: strongest in technical, recursive, low-visibility domains, weakest exactly where the headlines look.

activities.caption: find the line the command theory cannot survive
activities.name: ilAustinSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary smuggles in the command-theory fallacy — click it:
lines: Austin's objection: no sovereign, therefore no law.
States invoke the rules to justify and accuse.
They argue about what the rules require — and comply in the overwhelming run of cases.
They build institutions to apply them.
Because no police force answers to it, the system is not law at all.
config.correction: A system that functions as law among its subjects is law — the objection is a definition, not an argument.
config.why: The working question was never "is it law?" but "when does it bite?" — reciprocity, reputation, stakes: a quantitative answer.

activities.anchor: its record is better than its reputation
activities.caption: pair each bench with its way of getting obeyed
activities.name: ilCourtsMatch

config.prompt: Four benches, four ways of getting obeyed — pair each with its mechanism:

pairs.right: jurisdiction by consent; Security Council politics gate execution (Nicaragua)
a treaty court for individuals — Rome Statute 2002; major powers sit outside
binding adjudication backed by authorised retaliation — Appellate Body paralysed since 2019, MPIA the patch
individual petition, and domestic courts that execute the judgments

config.why: State responsibility is the connective law: the ILC Articles codify when a breach triggers cessation and reparation, and what lawful countermeasures — self-help short of force — the injured state may take.

activities.anchor: the court's name is global and its mandate sounds universal
activities.caption: bet on the treaty court's reach
activities.name: ilIccPredict

config.q: An atrocity happens inside a major power that never joined the Rome Statute. Can the ICC prosecute its head of state?
choices: Yes — the statute reaches every head of state on earth
No — jurisdiction rests on consent: the accused's state or the crime's territory must be a party, or the Security Council must refer
Yes, but only after a General Assembly vote
config.why: It is a treaty court, not a world criminal court: with the US, Russia, China and India outside, reach stops at some of the most powerful borders — which is why the early docket skewed toward weaker states and selectivity became the standing legitimacy problem.

activities.anchor: The compliance literature's findings deserve their quantitative summary
activities.caption: drag the divider — teeth versus domestic courts
activities.name: ilDeepCompare

config.prompt: What explains the variance in obedience rates? Drag between the theories:

before.label: The intuitive bet: regime strength
before.text: Stronger institutions with sharper enforcement teeth should produce better obedience.

after.label: The finding: domestic institutionalisation
after.text: Obedience tracks courts, implementing legislation and mobilised publics — trade obligations performed near-universally; even ritual-criticised human-rights reporting shows behavioural effects where constituencies can litigate.

config.why: The transnational legal process account: internalisation through interaction, interpretation and friction — empower domestic actors rather than relying on international enforcement; the European model's deepest lesson, now the template every new regime argues about.
